intro: This unit tells stories about two wise teachers from old China. One is Laozi, the Old Master. The other is Zhuangzi, who told puzzling stories.
You will hear how Laozi left a book at a gate. You will hear about a butterfly dream and a crooked tree. You will learn the word Dao, which means the Way.
By the end, you can retell these stories. You can say what the Dao means. You can ask your own 'what if?' questions. You can share them.
bigQuestion: What do the stories of Laozi and Zhuangzi help us wonder about?

timeline.t: Laozi, the Old Master, cares for old writings
Laozi rides west on a water buffalo, the stories say
A gatekeeper asks him to write his wisdom down
He leaves a short book: the Daodejing
Later, Zhuangzi tells funny, puzzling stories
Zhuangzi and Huizi talk about happy fish
Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly
A crooked tree grows old and gives shade to all

the short book of wisdom connected with Laozi
the Way; a path that the Daodejing says all things follow
a person who follows the teachings of the Dao
soft and kind, not rough
a teacher in old China who told funny, puzzling stories
pictures and stories in your mind while you sleep
not the same as others

test.why: The Daodejing is the book connected with Laozi.

test.why: Gentle kindness is the first treasure.

test.why: In chapter 2, he dreamed he was a butterfly.

Many Daoists honor Laozi with great respect.

write.prompt: Tell or draw: Which story made you wonder the most, the butterfly dream (Zhuangzi, chapter 2) or the useless tree (Zhuangzi, chapter 4)? Tell what happens and what readers say it means.
tips: Use one unit word, like Dao or different.
Draw a picture if it helps you.

title: Stories of Laozi and Zhuangzi

chapters.title: The Old Master Rides West
chapters.bigQuestion: What did the stories say the Old Master left behind for us?

story.title: Stopped at the Gate
story.kicker: A gatekeeper asks an old man for one last gift.
paragraphs: Long ago, an old man rode slowly toward the west. The stories say he rode a water buffalo. His beard was long and white. He was leaving China for good.
At a mountain pass there was a gate. A gatekeeper stood there. He saw the old man coming. He knew this man was a wise teacher.
'Please wait,' said the gatekeeper. 'Before you go, write down your wisdom. Then we will still have it.' The old man thought for a moment. Then he said yes.
The old man sat and wrote. He wrote a short book in two parts. He gave it to the gatekeeper. Then he rode on through the gate. The old story says no one knows where he went.
story.think: Why do you think the gatekeeper wanted the old man to write his wisdom down?

lessons.title: The Old Master
lessons.mainIdea: Laozi means the Old Master. Stories say he was a wise teacher in old China.
reading: The old man in the story is called Laozi. Lao means old. Zi means master. So Laozi means the Old Master.
The old stories say he worked in a king's library. He took care of old writings. He was quiet and wise. Some say he was very, very old.

words.d: the Old Master; a wise teacher in stories from old China

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at a quiet room full of bamboo scrolls. They are rolled up and stacked on shelves. An old man with a white beard reads one slowly. He smiles.
look.prompt: What job do you think the old man has?

check.q: What does Laozi mean?
check.why: Lao means old and zi means master.

check.q: Where do the stories say Laozi worked?
check.why: The old stories say he cared for old writings in a library.

check.q: What was Laozi like in the stories?
check.why: The stories tell of a quiet, wise old teacher.

lessons.title: Was He One Real Person?
lessons.mainIdea: Historians are not sure Laozi was one real person, and people have told his story in many ways.
reading: Laozi lived so long ago that no one is sure about him. Historians are people who study the past. Many say they do not know if he was one real person.
Some think his book grew from many wise teachers. Others follow the old stories. People can ask this question kindly and with respect.

words.d: a person who studies what happened long ago

look.title: Two Ideas
look.text: Idea one: One old teacher named Laozi wrote the whole book. Idea two: Many wise teachers added to the book over a long time. Historians talk about both ideas.
look.prompt: Why might it be hard to know about someone from long, long ago?

check.q: What is a historian?
choices: A person who studies the past
check.why: Historians study what happened long ago.

check.q: Are historians sure Laozi was one real person?
check.why: Many historians say they do not know for sure.

check.q: What is one idea about how the book was made?
choices: Many wise teachers added to it
It was found on the moon
check.why: Some think the book grew from many teachers over time.

lessons.title: A Gift for the Gatekeeper
lessons.mainIdea: An old story says a gatekeeper asked Laozi to write his wisdom before he left.
reading: An old history book tells the gate story. It was written by Sima Qian, a Chinese historian. He wrote it more than 2,000 years ago.
He wrote that Laozi was leaving. A gatekeeper asked for his wisdom. Laozi wrote a book of about 5,000 words. Then he left.

words.d: a person who watches a gate and lets people through

look.title: The Gate Story
look.text: Laozi was leaving. The keeper of the pass said: before you go, please write a book for me. So Laozi wrote a book in two parts, about 5,000 words long, and went away.
look.cite: Sima Qian, Records of the Historian (Shiji), chapter 63, retold simply
look.prompt: What did the gatekeeper ask for?

check.q: Who asked Laozi to write his wisdom down?
check.why: In the story, the keeper of the pass asked him.

check.q: About how many words did the book have?
check.why: The old history says about 5,000 words.

check.q: Who wrote down the gate story long ago?
check.why: The historian Sima Qian wrote the story.

lessons.title: The Daodejing
lessons.mainIdea: The book people connect with Laozi is called the Daodejing.
reading: The book in the story is called the Daodejing. You say it like 'dow-duh-jing.' It is also spelled Tao Te Ching.
It has 81 short parts called chapters. Many are like little poems. People all over the world read it today.

words.d: the short book of wisdom connected with Laozi
one part of a book

look.title: A Small Book
look.cite: Traditional count of the Daodejing; Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 63
look.prompt: How many chapters does the Daodejing have?

check.q: What is the book called?
check.why: The book connected with Laozi is the Daodejing.

check.q: How many chapters does it have?
check.why: The Daodejing has 81 short chapters.

check.q: What are many chapters like?
check.why: Many chapters read like short poems.

lessons.title: Dao Means the Way
lessons.mainIdea: Dao means the Way. The Daodejing says the Way is like a path all things follow.
reading: Dao means the Way, like a road or path. The Daodejing uses it for something big. It says all of nature follows the Way.
The book says the Way is hard to put in words. It says to be quiet and watch nature. Then you may learn from it.

words.d: the Way; a path that the Daodejing says all things follow

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at a river flowing down a hill. It goes around rocks. It never rushes back up. The seasons come in order: spring, summer, fall, winter.
look.prompt: How does nature seem to follow a way or path?

check.q: What does Dao mean?
check.why: Dao means the Way, like a path.

check.q: What does the Daodejing say follows the Way?
check.why: The book says all things follow the Way.

check.q: What does the book say about the Way?
choices: It is easy to say in one word
It is hard to put in words
It is a kind of food
check.why: The Daodejing says the Way is hard to put in words.

lessons.title: Gentle and Simple
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing teaches three treasures: kindness, using little and not pushing to be first.
reading: One chapter names three treasures. The first is kindness, or gentleness. The second is using little. The third is not pushing to be first.
Daoists, people who follow the Dao, value these treasures. Many Daoists also honor Laozi at temples. They treat him with great respect.

words.d: soft and kind, not rough
a person who follows the teachings of the Dao

look.title: Three Treasures
look.text: I have three treasures. I hold them close. The first is gentle kindness. The second is using little. The third is not rushing to be first.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 67, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Which treasure would help on the playground? Why?

check.q: How many treasures does chapter 67 name?
check.why: Daodejing 67 names three treasures.

check.q: Which is one of the three treasures?
check.why: Gentleness, or kindness, is the first treasure.

check.q: Who is a Daoist?
choices: A person who follows the teachings of the Dao
check.why: Daoists follow the teachings of the Dao.

review.why: Lao means old and zi means master.

review.q: In the stories, what did Laozi ride west?
review.why: The stories say he rode a water buffalo.

review.q: What did the gatekeeper ask for?
review.why: He asked Laozi to write down his wisdom.
It is the short book connected with Laozi.

review.q: What do historians say about Laozi?
choices: They are not sure he was one real person
review.why: Many historians are not sure he was one real person.

chapters.title: The Butterfly Dream and the Useless Tree
chapters.bigQuestion: What can a puzzling story help us wonder about?

story.title: Waking Up Wondering
story.kicker: A man dreams he is a butterfly, then wakes up puzzled.
paragraphs: A man named Zhuangzi lay down for a nap. He fell asleep. He began to dream. In his dream, he was a butterfly. It was a warm day.
He flew over flowers. He floated on the wind. He was happy. He did not remember being a man at all. He was just a butterfly.
Then he woke up. He looked at his hands. He was Zhuangzi again! But he was puzzled. He scratched his head and wondered. He sat very still.
Was he Zhuangzi, who had dreamed he was a butterfly? Or was he a butterfly, now dreaming he was Zhuangzi? He did not know. He smiled at the puzzle.
story.think: Have you ever had a dream that felt real? What did you wonder when you woke up?

lessons.title: A Teacher Who Told Stories
lessons.mainIdea: Zhuangzi was a teacher in old China who told funny, puzzling stories.
reading: Zhuangzi lived in China more than 2,000 years ago. He lived after Confucius. He was a teacher and a thinker.
Zhuangzi loved to tell stories. Some were funny. Some were puzzling. His stories are collected in a book. The book is called the Zhuangzi, too.

words.d: a teacher in old China who told funny, puzzling stories

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at a man sitting by a river. He is laughing. Talking animals, tall trees and a giant bird fill his stories. Friends sit around him and listen.
look.prompt: Why might a teacher use funny stories to teach?

check.q: Who was Zhuangzi?
check.why: Zhuangzi was a teacher who told funny, puzzling stories.

check.q: Did Zhuangzi live before or after Confucius?
choices: At the same time as us
check.why: Zhuangzi lived after Confucius.

check.q: What is his book called?
check.why: His book has his name: the Zhuangzi.

lessons.title: Happy Fish
lessons.mainIdea: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi liked to argue about big questions, like how we know things.
reading: Zhuangzi had a friend named Huizi. They walked on a bridge. Zhuangzi said, 'Look how happy the fish are!'
Huizi asked, 'You are not a fish. How do you know they are happy?' The friends kept talking. They liked puzzles like this.

words.d: Zhuangzi's friend who liked to argue about ideas

look.title: On the Bridge
look.text: Zhuangzi said, 'The fish swim so freely. They are happy.' Huizi said, 'You are not a fish. How can you know they are happy?'
look.cite: Zhuangzi, chapter 17, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: How do you think Zhuangzi could answer Huizi?

check.q: Who was Huizi?
check.why: Huizi was Zhuangzi's friend who liked to argue.

check.q: Where were the friends walking?
check.why: They were on a bridge over the water.

check.q: What did Huizi ask?
choices: How do you know the fish are happy?
check.why: Huizi asked how Zhuangzi could know the fish were happy.

lessons.title: Man or Butterfly?
lessons.mainIdea: Zhuangzi told of dreaming he was a butterfly and waking up unsure which one he was.
reading: The butterfly story is in chapter 2 of the Zhuangzi. It is very short. But people have talked about it for a long time.
Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly. He wakes up. He wonders which is real. The story does not give an answer. It leaves us wondering.

words.d: pictures and stories in your mind while you sleep

look.title: The Butterfly Dream
look.text: Once Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, flying happily. He woke up and was Zhuangzi. He did not know: was he a man who dreamed of a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming of a man?
look.cite: Zhuangzi, chapter 2, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Does the story give an answer? Why do you think so?

check.q: What did Zhuangzi dream he was?
check.why: In chapter 2, he dreams he is a butterfly.

check.q: What did he wonder when he woke up?
check.why: He wondered if he was a man or a butterfly dreaming.

check.q: Does the story give a clear answer?
choices: Yes, it was all a game
check.why: The story leaves the question open.

lessons.title: Asking What If
lessons.mainIdea: Zhuangzi's stories invite readers to ask 'what if?' and look at things in new ways.
reading: Zhuangzi's stories ask 'what if?' What if things are not what they seem? What if we looked from a new side?
Readers have understood the stories in many ways. Some say they teach us to be open. Others say they help us feel less worried.

words.d: to think about something and ask questions

look.title: Look Again
look.text: A puddle looks small to you. To an ant, it is a big lake. A hill looks tall to a mouse. To a bird high in the sky, it looks tiny.
look.prompt: How can the same thing look different to different living things?

check.q: What question do Zhuangzi's stories ask?
check.why: His stories invite us to ask 'what if?'

check.q: What do some readers say the stories teach?
choices: To be open to new ways of seeing
check.why: Some readers say the stories teach us to be open.

check.q: Why does a puddle look like a lake to an ant?
check.why: Things look different depending on who is looking.

lessons.title: A Tree No One Wanted
lessons.mainIdea: In a Zhuangzi story, carpenters passed by a big crooked tree because its wood was no good for building.
reading: A carpenter walked by a giant tree. It was crooked and bumpy. Its wood was no good for boats or houses. He walked on by.
Because no one cut it down, the tree grew very old. It grew huge. Its branches spread wide over the land.

words.d: a person who builds things out of wood
bent, not straight

look.title: The Big Tree
look.text: A carpenter saw a huge tree by a shrine. He did not stop. 'Its wood is no good,' he said. 'Boats made of it would sink. That is why it has lived so long.'
look.cite: Zhuangzi, chapter 4, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1891)
look.prompt: Why did the tree get to grow so old?

check.q: Why did the carpenter walk past the tree?
choices: Its wood was no good for building
check.why: In chapter 4, the carpenter says its wood is no good.

check.q: What happened to the tree?
choices: It grew very old and big
check.why: No one cut it down, so it grew old and huge.

check.q: What does crooked mean?
check.why: Crooked means bent, not straight.

lessons.title: Shade for Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: Zhuangzi's tree story suggests that being different can be good in its own way.
reading: The crooked tree gave wide shade. People and animals rested under it. It was useful in a new way.
Readers say the story shows that being different can be good. Something that seems useless may help in a surprising way.

words.d: not helpful for a job, or seeming that way
not the same as others

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at the giant crooked tree on a hot day. A farmer naps in its shade. Birds build nests high up. Children play around its bumpy roots.
look.prompt: Name three ways the 'useless' tree is helping.

check.q: How did the crooked tree help?
check.why: It gave shade where people and animals rested.

check.q: What do readers say the story shows?
check.why: Readers say the story shows being different can be good.

check.q: Which book has the useless tree story?
check.why: The useless tree is a story in the Zhuangzi.

review.q: What did Zhuangzi dream he was?
review.why: In chapter 2, he dreams he is a butterfly.

review.q: Who was Zhuangzi's friend on the bridge?
review.why: Huizi talked with him about the happy fish.

review.q: Why did no one cut down the big tree?
review.why: Carpenters thought its wood was no good for building.

review.q: What did the crooked tree give?
review.why: It spread wide and gave shade to everyone.

review.q: What kind of stories did Zhuangzi tell?
What question do his stories often ask?
review.why: His stories invite readers to wonder 'what if?'
